title: Five Things Worth Remembering
teaser: Six days in. Before tomorrow's silence, look back. Five short sections — one per day — surfacing what the week was actually saying.
theme: Recap and integration. No new teaching — only the five claims of the week, laid out side by side, so the reader can see the shape of what has been arriving.
framework: Day 6 — recap. Spacious, low-velocity. A hand of cards laid on the table.
scriptureReference: (week's anchor passages — Mark 1:1; Isaiah 52:7; 1 Corinthians 15:3-5; Romans 1:17; Acts 8:36)

modules.heading: WHAT WE'VE WALKED THROUGH
modules.intro:
Six days in. Before we sit in silence tomorrow, look back at what the week has been saying.

No new teaching today. Five short sections — one per day — surfacing the central claim of each. Read them slowly. The point is not to learn anything new. The point is to see the whole hand of cards laid out on the table at once. Some of these will land harder than they did the first time. Some will sound, today, like they were written for someone other than the person who read them four days ago. That is fine. The week was meant to do its work in layers, not in a single read.

The series has been called What is Euangelion? — an old Greek word the church inherited and, over twenty centuries, mostly buried under the wear of repetition. The work of the week was not to define the word once and move on. It was to set the word down in five different rooms and let the reader walk around it slowly. Day 1 put it back into the public square it came from. Day 2 dug under it for the older Hebrew shape underneath. Day 3 named what the word actually carries — a person, not a system. Day 4 named the posture that fits a person. Day 5 closed the loop with a man on a road who had only just begun to hear it himself. What follows is a small map of those five rooms.

If one of these stops you, stop. Do not move on for the sake of moving on. Sit with the one that lands hardest. That is the one the week has been doing its work through. The runner who has been running through these readings has been running toward you specifically; he does not work in averages.

days.title: A Word You Already Know in a Language You Don't
days.key_insight: Euangelion was not, in its first life, a religious word. It was a herald's word — the kind of announcement a runner carried from a battlefield to a city that had not yet heard, the kind of phrase chiseled into stone for the birth of a Caesar. Mark, writing in Rome in the AD 60s, borrowed the word on purpose. He was making a political claim before he made a theological one: the world has a different king than it thought it did, and the herald is already running.

days.title: The Word Before the Word
days.key_insight: The Greek word the New Testament uses had a Hebrew shadow that ran centuries before it. Besorah — the runner's report, the watchman's cry. Isaiah's exiles in Babylon were already on the wall, scanning the horizon for the figure with beautiful feet who would come over the ridge with news that the captivity was ending. The Septuagint translators, working two centuries before Christ, had already stitched the Greek word into Isaiah. The gospel was a Hebrew concept before it was a Greek word. Same announcement, older mouth, longer waiting.

days.title: The Messenger and the Message Are the Same Person
days.key_insight: This is the center of the week. Other faiths and frameworks have a teacher who delivers a message — and the message can be detached from the teacher and held on its own. The Eightfold Path stands without the Buddha; the Meditations stand without Marcus. Christianity is structurally different. The messenger and the message are the same person. The four-line creed Paul received within five years of the crucifixion — died, buried, raised, appeared — has no extractable doctrine that survives the removal of the person. The good news is not what Jesus taught. Jesus is the good news.

days.title: Empty Hands, Not Full Ones
days.key_insight: If the message is a person and what He has done is finished, the only fitting response is to receive Him with open hands. Faith — pistis in Greek, emunah in Hebrew — is not private belief held without evidence. It is trust. The kind of trust that puts weight on another person and walks forward as if the person can be relied on. Luther, writing to a young friend coming apart under his own scruples, named the medicine: bring the real, unsanitized self, and let your trust in Christ be stronger than the sin you are bringing to Him. The righteousness in the verse is not a wall to climb. It is a robe already laid on the chair. The clenched hand of producing cannot, at the same moment, be the open hand of receiving.

days.title: An Open Road, Not an Altar Call
days.key_insight: The Bible itself almost never closes a gospel announcement with a sales close. It closes them on a road, between two strangers, with a question the listener asks. The Ethiopian official, riding home from Jerusalem, reading Isaiah 53 alone in his chariot, looked up and asked, 'What is there to prevent me?' That sentence — small, honest, in motion — is how the news lands in a real life. Not in a stadium. Not in a closing argument. In one person on a road, with something open in their hands, asking the smallest possible next question. Not a decision today. A door that stays open.

modules.integration_question:
Which of these landed hardest? Sit with that one.

Not the one you think you should pick. Not the one that sounds most theological. The one that, when you read it again just now, did something small in your chest that you cannot quite explain. That is the one the week has been doing its work through. Stay with it for a few minutes before you close the page. Notice what you notice.

If more than one landed — if two or three of them seem to be working on you at once — that is also fine. Pick the one the week began with for you. Some readers were stopped on Day 1 by the simple recovery of the word. Some had been waiting their whole life to hear Day 3. Some did not know they had been climbing until they got to Day 4. Some, finally, sat down on the road of Day 5.

Wherever you are, you are not behind. The whole point of the chiasm is that the week loops. Day 1 and Day 5 say the same thing in different vocabularies. Day 2 and Day 4 say the same thing in different vocabularies. Day 3 is the hinge. If only one paragraph of the week stays with you, let it be the one in the middle: the messenger and the message are the same person.

For today, no decision. No new program. No quiz. Sit with the one card that has the most weight in your hand right now. The runner has reached the gate. The chariot is on the road. The water is by the side of the road. Tomorrow is rest.
modules.transition_to_sabbath: Tomorrow, no teaching. Just presence. One scripture, one prayer, one invitation. The work of the week has been words; the work of tomorrow is silence. You have read enough. Sit in what was read.

modules.title: A Prayer of Integration
modules.prayerText:
God of the runner and the road, God of the watchman on the wall and the chariot in the desert —

I have read words for five days. Some landed. Some did not. Some landed in places I have not had words for in a long time.

I do not know what to do with all of it yet. I do not have to. The week is not asking me to settle anything tonight. It is asking me to sit with what arrived.

If any of it is true — if the messenger really is the message, if the work really is finished, if the road really is open — please do the slow work in me that I cannot do in myself. I am willing to keep my hands open. I am willing to keep reading. I am willing to be on the road tomorrow without forcing a destination today.

Let the one that landed hardest go on landing. Let the rest of them keep working underneath. I am here. I am still here. Amen.
